title: Strongly polynomial near-linear negative-weight shortest paths
formal: Do there exist a uniform randomized comparison-addition algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(k\ge0\) that compute all exact distances from one specified source in every directed graph with arbitrary real arc lengths and no negative directed cycle, using at most \(C(m+n)(\log(n+2))^{k}\) operations and succeeding with probability at least \(2/3\)?
definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Arc lengths may be positive, zero or negative. A path length is the sum of its arc lengths; the empty path has length zero. Output the minimum source-to-vertex path length for every vertex, or an infinity marker if unreachable. The promise excludes negative cycles anywhere in the graph. Use a uniform comparison-addition RAM. Real cells contain exact real numbers and support copying, addition, subtraction and comparison at unit cost; fixed rational program constants are allowed. Real multiplication, division, floor, bit extraction and conversion of an input-dependent real to an integer are not primitives. Integer control and address words have \(d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(d\), with unit-cost Boolean operations, shifts, comparison and arithmetic on words. Integer operations cannot inspect real encodings. A fixed finite program receives no advice or free tables. Memory accesses, control, preprocessing and output all count. Bounds are uniform over all real edge values. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The operation bound is independent of all magnitudes and numerical encoding lengths. On rational inputs, intermediate values must have bit length polynomial in the total binary input length; this is the usual additional encoding condition for strong polynomiality.

context_blocks.text: Negative lengths allow shortest paths to express costs, credits and difference constraints. They make the numerical model essential: a graph-size bound uniform over real weights is stronger than a bound depending on the number of bits in integer weights.

Bernstein, Nanongkai and Wulff-Nilsen obtained near-linear integer-weight shortest paths with a \(\log W\) dependence. Bringmann, Cassis and Fischer improve the logarithmic factors and explicitly ask whether strong polynomiality can remove that dependence.

The February 2026 preprint by Li, Li and Zhang gives \(n^{2+o(1)}\) time for real weights. This is almost linear for dense graphs, but it neither has polylogarithmic overhead nor gives the requested sparse-graph bound.
Mareš supplies the shortest-path background; the endpoint and status distinctions here come from the later research papers.

why: Removing numerical scaling dependence in a nearly input-linear bound would settle a central gap in exact shortest-path computation over arbitrary real data.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.

progress.text: Near-linear algorithms become available for integer weights with a numerical scaling factor.
The integer-weight near-linear bound is derandomized; the weight dependence remains.
A preprint states an \(n^{2+o(1)}\) real-weight algorithm, leaving the general near-linear target open.

status_note: Sources and subsequent-result searches checked on 13 September 2026. The cited results leave this target unanswered; this is a bounded literature review, not an exhaustive certification of current openness. The approved real-weight formulation of the strong-polynomial endpoint fixes bounded error and worst-case operation cost. It is not the solved near-linear integer-weight question.

sentences: The input is a directed graph with arbitrary real edge lengths and no negative cycle.
The task is to compute all distances from one source exactly.
The question asks for near-linear comparison-addition time independent of weight magnitudes.
Near-linear integer-weight algorithms and almost-quadratic real-weight algorithms leave this general target unanswered.
A resolution would close a central gap between numerical scaling and strongly polynomial graph computation.
